papers.title: Browser-Based Video Supports Scalable Computer Vision Analysis for Open Surgical Skill Assessment
papers.abstract: Purpose: Objective assessment of open surgical skills remains limited by expert availability. Machine learning (ML)-based hand keypoint detection offers potential for automated, on-demand assessment, but performance in accessible browser-based recording environments (laptop-webcam video recorded in a web browser) is unknown. We hypothesized that browser-based recordings would achieve acceptable keypoint localization (percentage of correct keypoints [PCK] >70%). Methods: Retrospective technical validation of prospectively collected video from 14 PGY-1 interns at one academic center (July to August 2024). We annotated 203 frames (101 browser-based, 1280x720/854x480; 102 overhead, 3840x2160/1920x1080), yielding 6,232 ground-truth keypoints. An internally developed pipeline and MediaPipe Hands were evaluated. The primary endpoint was PCK normalized to the index-proximal bone; bounding-box-normalized PCK, detection rate, and per-region accuracy were also evaluated. Results: Primary PCK, normalized to a fixed anatomical hand scale, was 85.9% (95% CI, 80.3-91.0) for browser-based recordings and 81.5% (95% CI, 76.7-87.0) for overhead recordings. Secondary bounding-box-normalized PCK showed a similar pattern (91.6% vs 90.6%), and detection rates were high in both environments (94.9% vs 97.7%). In contrast, MediaPipe detection rates were only 5.3% for browser-based recordings and 15.4% for overhead recordings, resulting in substantially lower accuracy. Conclusion: Hand keypoint detection performance was comparable between browser-based and overhead recordings using the internally developed pipeline. These findings suggest that browser-based video acquisition can provide data of sufficient quality for ML-based hand keypoint detection, offering a scalable pathway for surgical skill assessment without specialized recording hardware.

papers.title: Spine Endoscopic Atlas-Tissue: multi-class anatomical segmentation in endoscopic spine surgery
papers.abstract: Spine Endoscopic Atlas-Tissue (SEA-T) is a multicenter dataset for pixel-level multi-class semantic segmentation in endoscopic spine surgery. It contains 3,310 expert-annotated frames from 65 patients (1,663 cervical frames from 39 patients; 1,647 lumbar frames from 26 patients) across three centers, plus 11,155 unlabeled frames. Annotations cover nine classes - upper/lower lamina, ligamentum flavum, dural sac, nerve root, adipose tissue, muscle, disc material, and instrument channel - created in 3D Slicer under multi-stage quality control, with Fleiss' kappa of 0.789. The annotated data are split by center, procedure, and anatomy into Center A training, internal validation, internal test, and held-out sub-cohorts, with Center B and Center C external tests; unlabeled frames are kept separate. Baselines spanning convolutional and foundation-model paradigms - nnU-Net v2, CaraNet, MedSAM2, and the SAM-based MA-SAM baseline - report Dice-based evaluation and reveal center-dependent domain shift. SEA-T is released with native-resolution PNG images, NRRD/MRML masks, RGB overlay images for annotation review, and metadata.

papers.title: Individualised and Time-Dependent Prediction of Recurrence After Colorectal Cancer Liver Metastases Resection
papers.abstract: IntroductionTreatment strategies for colorectal cancer liver metastases (CRLM) are increasingly complex, driving interest in advanced prognostic tools. Externally validated benchmarks based on established clinical risk scores are needed to contextualise emerging models. However, existing scores remain difficult to apply and compare, because they provide categorical risk strata rather than individualised probabilities, and because model parameters are rarely published. Here, we validate and recalibrate seven established risk scores to derive individualised recurrence probabilities for future score benchmarking. MethodPatients undergoing index CRLM resection from two tertiary centres were included: Karolinska University Hospital (retrospective KaroLiver cohort [2013-2021, follow-up to 2025, n=709]) and Oslo University Hospital (OSLO-COMET trial cohort [2012-2016, follow-up to 2022, n=198]). Performance of the GAME, m-CS, Fong, Nordlinger, Nagashima, Konopke and Helsinki scores was assessed using recurrence-free survival as the primary outcome. ResultsAmong 709 patients in KaroLiver (median age 67 years [IQR 59-74]; 434 men [61%]), 422 (60%) had synchronous metastases and 444 (63%) received neoadjuvant chemotherapy. All scores significantly stratified recurrence risk (log-rank P<0.001; time-dependent AUC 0.63-0.74 at 3 years), albeit with performance differences across time points. Recalibrated models showed good agreement between predicted and observed recurrence and were externally validated in OSLO-COMET with broadly comparable net benefit. Models were implemented in the online tool PLATO (Personalised Liver metastases risk AssessmenT in Oncology). ConclusionEstablished CRLM risk scores can be translated into individualised probabilistic recurrence estimates at clinically relevant time points, supporting patient communication, risk-adapted surveillance and transparent benchmarking of next-generation prognostic models.

papers.title: Prediction of elective surgical red blood cell transfusion reveals surgeon-level variation
papers.abstract: BACKGROUNDPreoperative prediction of red blood cell (RBC) transfusion in elective surgery serves two complementary purposes: enabling patient blood management (PBM) interventions before surgery and supporting blood product supply planning for elective lists. Beyond patient risk factors, individual surgeon practice may also contribute to transfusion rates, but this effect has not been fully quantified. STUDY DESIGN AND METHODSIn a retrospective cohort of 279,905 elective surgical procedures at Helsinki University Hospital (2021-2025), we trained four gradient-boosted tree (CatBoost) models crossing patient factors with procedure group and pseudonymised surgeon identity. All predictors were restricted to data available seven or more days before scheduled surgery. The primary outcome was any allogeneic RBC transfusion from operating-room entry through seven postoperative days. Discrimination was assessed by the area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) on a held-out 20% test set. Surgeon-level effects were characterised by Shapley additive explanation (SHAP) values. RESULTSThe transfusion rate was 2.2%. The patient-only model achieved AUPRC 0.261 (no-skill baseline 0.022). Adding surgeon identity to the procedure-adjusted model increased AUPRC from 0.440 to 0.472 (+0.032; 95% CI 0.020-0.044), raising lift from 20.3 to 21.7. Surgeon identity was the third most important of 72 features by permutation importance. DISCUSSIONThe operating surgeon was associated with RBC transfusion beyond patient and procedure factors, and surgeon identity was the third most important predictor in a deployment-realistic model using only data available a week before surgery. This information is readily available from routine records and could support PBM audit and blood supply planning for elective surgery.

papers.title: Surgical Revision of Deep Brain Stimulation After Suboptimal Clinical Outcomes: A Systematic Review and Exploratory Meta-analysis
papers.abstract: BackgroundSome patients obtain less benefit than expected from deep brain stimulation (DBS) despite optimized programming. We systematically reviewed the outcomes of surgical revision in this setting. MethodsFollowing PRISMA 2020, we searched PubMed, Embase and Scopus to October 2026 for studies of lead repositioning, replacement, added (rescue) leads or target switching performed for inadequate benefit or stimulation-related adverse effects; revision for infection or hardware failure was excluded. Outcomes were pooled with random-effects models, and certainty was rated with GRADE. ResultsSeventeen case series (approximately 149 patients) were included. Across 14 studies (95 patients), 81% (95% CI 68-91%) improved meaningfully, with similar estimates for same-target revision (82%) and for added or switched leads (79%). In Parkinson disease, the off-medication/on-stimulation motor score fell by 15.6 points after lead revision (95% CI -22.6 to -8.6; four studies). Benefit was greatest when a lead outside the dorsolateral subthalamic nucleus was corrected and levodopa response was preserved. Seven studies reported surgical or hardware complications, and two deaths occurred. Certainty of evidence was very low. ConclusionsMost published revised patients improve, but the evidence derives from small uncontrolled series. Revision should follow imaging, hardware checks and exhaustive reprogramming, within multidisciplinary review.

papers.title: Quantitative Shape Analysis Supports the Use of Aortic Arch Stent Grafts in Complex Aortic Geometries
papers.abstract: IntroductionTraditional thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) relies on distal landing zones beyond the left common carotid artery, which may underperform in patients with complex aortic anatomy. The Nexus Aortic Arch Stent Graft enables proximal landing zones in the ascending aorta, expanding endovascular options for challenging arch pathology. This study applies a geometrically focused framework using fluctuation in total integrated Gaussian curvature ({delta}K), a size-invariant metric of surface topology, to evaluate Nexus performance across diverse aortic morphologies. MethodsPre-operative CT imaging was analyzed for 27 patients treated with the Nexus device and 37 treated with traditional TEVAR (proximal landing zones 2/3). CT scans from 215 patients with non-pathologic aortas served as controls. Two-dimensional aortic surface meshes were constructed to calculate{delta} K and mean aortic radius, while tortuosity index was derived from the centerline. Nexus data were mapped into a previously established size-shape feature space to assess predicted outcomes. TEVAR failure was defined as reintervention or death due to aneurysmal growth, endoleak, dissection extension, or rupture. Correlation and clustering analyses evaluated relationships between aortic morphology and outcomes. A scale-sampling approach captured the multiscale nature of aortic geometry while reducing sensitivity to mesh resolution and partitioning. ResultsThe Traditional TEVAR cohort had a significantly lower success rate than the Nexus cohort (51.4% vs. 85.2%, p = 0.005). Traditional TEVAR was particularly less effective in patients with elevated{delta} K and large mean radius, whereas the Nexus device demonstrated favorable outcomes even in anatomically complex aortas with similarly elevated{delta} K and radius values. Combining{delta} K and radius demonstrated distinct clustering patterns by pathology: 78.3% of chronic dissections occupied the high{delta} K/radius zone, while 70.6% of isolated aneurysms fell in the low{delta} K/radius zone (p <0.001).{delta} K provided unique morphological insight beyond size, whereas tortuosity index was less discriminative. Conclusion{delta}K offers a quantitative framework for assessing device performance across variable aortic anatomy. Endovascular arch repair using proximal ascending aortic landing zones, exemplified by the Nexus device, may provide a viable option in patients with complex geometry. This shape-size framework represents a step toward personalized patient selection and improved long-term outcomes.

papers.title: Routine Chest CTA Reliably Quantifies Left Ventricular Myocardial Mass
papers.abstract: BackgroundRoutine chest computed tomography angiography (CTA) is the primary imaging modality for thoracic aortic disease, yet cardiac information within these examinations remains underutilized. We evaluated whether left ventricular myocardial mass (LVMM) can be reliably quantified from routine non-electrocardiographically (ECG)-gated chest CTA and its application in thoracic aortic pathology. MethodsCTA scans were obtained from 257 patients without aortic disease and 181 patients with thoracic aortic aneurysm or dissection. LVMM was quantified using automated three-dimensional segmentation. In a separate 10-patient validation cohort, LVMM was compared across end-systolic, end-diastolic, and non-ECG-gated source reconstructions. CTA-derived LVMM was compared with published echocardiographic and cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) reference values using Cohens d. ResultsLVMM remained stable across cardiac phases and non-ECG-gated images (mean coefficient of variation, 2.4%), whereas left ventricular volume varied substantially (36.9%). CTA-derived LVMM demonstrated small effect sizes with the Penn method (d = 0.22) and moderate effect sizes with ASE linear (d = 0.67), area-length (d = 0.68), and CMR (d = 0.63). LVMM increased through young adulthood, with minimal association with age beyond 30 years. LVMM was comparable between patients with thoracic aneurysms and normal adults (140 {+/-} 43 g vs. 141 {+/-} 40 g; adjusted p = 1.0) but significantly greater in acute (199 {+/-} 61 g) and chronic (191 {+/-} 57 g) aortic dissection (both adjusted p < 0.001). ConclusionsRoutine non-ECG-gated chest CTA enables reliable automated LVMM quantification without additional imaging or radiation and may facilitate large-scale investigations of ventricular remodeling in thoracic aortic disease.

papers.title: Nasal CPAP is associated with increased midfacial retrusion in children with FGFR-related craniosynostoses: risk factors and biomechanical determinants
papers.abstract: BackgroundChildren with FGFR-related craniosynostoses frequently require prolonged nasal continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) for severe obstructive sleep apnea while definitive craniofacial procedures are delayed. We investigated whether sustained CPAP use alters midfacial growth and identified the morphological and biomechanical determinants of this effect. MethodsIn this retrospective observational study, we combined longitudinal 3D morphometric analyses of craniofacial shape in CPAP-treated and untreated children with FGFR-related craniosynostoses with experimental measurements of mask-induced forces and pressure distribution using 3D-printed patient-specific facial models instrumented with sensors. Multivariate analyses characterized growth trajectories, and structural equation modeling (SEM) disentangled the effects of three major risk factors: age, initial morphology, and CPAP duration. ResultsCPAP-treated patients exhibited a distinct growth trajectory characterized by greater midfacial retrusion than untreated patients with similar baseline morphology. Mask use generated mechanical loads of 6-10 N. Intentional overtightening markedly increased the total force applied to the face, but no notable difference was observed between expert and non-expert operators. Craniofacial morphology was the main determinant of force and pressure distributions and of growth response, identifying morphological risk factors. CPAP duration exaggerated these effects, particularly at younger ages. SEM supported links between morphology, mechanical loading, and deviation from expected growth. ConclusionsNasal CPAP is associated with additional midfacial growth deviation in children with FGFR-related craniosynostoses, with susceptibility strongly dependent on baseline morphology, treatment duration, and age at initiation. These findings support systematic craniofacial growth monitoring during prolonged CPAP and consideration of respiratory management and interface fit within longitudinal craniofacial treatment planning.

papers.title: Current Attitudes and Use Patterns of Large Language Models in Clinical Practice and Medical Education Among Trauma Providers
papers.abstract: IntroductionLarge language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in clinical practice and medical education, yet uncertainty remains regarding appropriate use, oversight, and potential effects on clinical reasoning and patient safety. This study examined current LLM use patterns, attitudes, perceived risks, and priorities for responsible integration among individuals engaged in trauma care, clinical guidance development, and medical education. MethodsParticipants attending the third Design for Implementation: The Future of Trauma Clinical Guidance and Research Conference (DFI) completed surveys examining LLM use, attitudes, perceived inhibitors to personal use, and clinical applications. During facilitated sessions, participants used open-ended note-taking guides to document their perspectives regarding LLM use in clinical practice, education, and guidance development. Survey data were analyzed descriptively, and qualitative responses were analyzed using rapid qualitative content analysis. Results77 participants completed the pre-conference survey; 62 clinicians provided data regarding clinical LLM use and attitudes. Among clinicians, 15% reported daily LLM use, whereas 26% reported never using LLMs. Respondents expressed strongest agreement with the need for regular quality auditing of LLM-supported clinical decisions. Among 52 post-conference survey respondents, 96% somewhat or strongly agreed that clinical training curricula should include education on LLM use. Barriers to LLM use included time required to verify accuracy, concern about patient harm, and insufficient training in appropriate prompting. Oualitative data came from 23 note-taking documents administered during the conference. Both positive and negative perspectives arose regarding AI use, centering on topics including efficiency gains, deskilling and never-skilling, governance and oversight, accuracy and hallucination, patient safety, and education. DiscussionDFI participants recognized efficiency and informational benefits of LLMs while identifying important concerns related to accuracy, patient safety, skill development, and governance. Findings support a need for institutional guidance, education in responsible LLM use, and evaluation of the incorporation of these technologies into clinical practice and health professions education. What is already known on this topicLLMs have become prevalent across professional domains in recent years, including medical education and clinical practice. What this study addsThrough interactive sessions, key stakeholders working predominantly at urban academic medical centers characterized the current ways in which they see LLMs being used most frequently and the concerns they have with this use. How this study might affect research, practice, or policyThis study demonstrates a need to further understand current use patterns of LLMs in medical education and clinical practice, which would be necessary to develop guidelines for use and/or the oversight that many stakeholders identified as necessary.

papers.title: Mortality Among Patients with Severe Traumatic Brain Injury: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
papers.abstract: BackgroundSevere traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a leading cause of trauma death, yet reported mortality varies widely. We estimated the pooled mortality of severe TBI and explored sources of variation. MethodsWe searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library and Google Scholar from inception to January 2026 (PROSPERO CRD420261417287). Observational and interventional studies reporting the number of deaths among patients with severe TBI (Glasgow Coma Scale [GCS] [≤]8) were eligible. Two reviewers independently selected studies, extracted data and assessed risk of bias with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Logit-transformed proportions were pooled with a DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model; we report 95% confidence intervals (CI) and 95% prediction intervals (PI). Heterogeneity was explored by subgroup analysis, meta-regression and pre-specified sensitivity analyses, and certainty was rated with GRADE for prognosis. ResultsTwenty-four studies (11,544 patients; 5,234 deaths) from 15 countries, published 2001-2024, were included. Study-level mortality ranged from 18.2% to 71.1%. Pooled mortality was 40.9% (95% CI 35.7-46.3%; I{superscript 2} = 96.3%), with a 95% PI of 18.9-67.2%. Mortality differed by region (p = 0.002): 47.1% (37.6-56.8%) in Africa, 44.5% (40.2-48.8%) in Europe, 38.6% (25.4-53.7%) in Asia and 31.6% (26.5-37.2%) in the Americas. Mortality did not differ significantly by country income group, outcome time point, age group or publication year. Estimates were robust to alternative random-effects estimators, leave-one-out analysis (range 39.6-41.7%) and restriction to studies with independently verified counts (41.7%) or low risk of bias (38.4%). Certainty of evidence was low. ConclusionsApproximately two in five patients with severe TBI die, but the wide prediction interval shows that the expected mortality in any single setting may lie anywhere between roughly one in five and two in three. Mortality was highest in African cohorts. Standardised definitions, outcome time points and reporting are needed to allow meaningful comparison across trauma systems.

papers.title: Increase in Surgical Case Mix Index Across a Multi-Hospital System with Structured Limited Surgeon Chart Review
papers.abstract: IntroductionHospitals face increasing financial pressures. Hospital reimbursement is tied to the Case Mix Index (CMI). The CMI is a measure of complexity of care provided by the hospital and the total reimbursement is the CMI multiplied by a base pay factor, multiplied by the total number of discharges from the hospital. The few studies in the literature have involved logistically complex attempts to improve documentation. We sought to determine whether limited, structured chart review by surgeons can improve CMI in a multihospital system. MethodsWe performed a prospective, observational study in a four-hospital academic medical system on all surgical patients from 10/2022 to 7/2026. Two clinically busy trauma surgeons performed limited structured chart reviews for select surgical patients. In the limited intervention period (1/2024-9/2024) this focused only on the trauma division. In the full intervention period (10/2024-7/2026) expanded to all surgical patients across the system. The main outcome was surgical case mix index (CMI). ResultsA total of 35,695 patients were included (13,811 pre-intervention, 9,337 limited intervention, 12,547 full intervention). CMI increased significantly among surgical patients across the whole system (2.68 (95%CI 2.65-2.71) to 2.87 (95%CI 2.82-2.92) to 2.97 (95%CI 2.93-3.01), ANOVA p <0.001). Overall length of stay was unchanged among surgical patients across the whole system. The estimated increase in revenue per patient attributable to this intervention was $3,912 in surgical patients across the system. ConclusionHaving trauma surgeons review targeted surgical patients for high value documentation capture significantly enhanced the CMI and estimated revenue of surgical services across a multi-hospital integrated health system. Such documentation reviews may represent a practical method to improve hospital documentation and revenue. Level of EvidenceLevel IV Study TypeProspective cohort study with historical controls Key MessagesWhat is already known on this topic: Documentation is critically important for hospital billing. Previous studies in trauma and acute care surgery have shown that large, intensive, and dedicated interventions can improve documentation and improve revenue generation. What this study adds: By creating a list of Major Comorbidity/Complication (MCC) and Comorbidity/Complication (CC) codes for targeted review, two clinically busy trauma surgeons were able to perform limited, targeted chart review with significant improvement in DRG capture and Case Mix Index. How this study might affect research, practice or policy: Improvements in documentation are facilitated by the targeted list of MCC and CC codes that other centers can use to improve their DRG capture, further demonstrating the financial benefit of a trauma and acute care surgery service.

papers.title: Bench Testing of an 8 N Slip Resistance Specification for the Handle Shaft Locking Interface of an Articulated Laparoscopic Instrument
papers.abstract: BackgroundArticulated laparoscopic instruments require a reliable mechanical connection between the handle and shaft to maintain the intended instrument configuration during surgical manipulation. The handle-shaft locking interface should resist unintended relative displacement under external loading. However, the appropriateness of a specific slip-resistance threshold must be evaluated in relation to the instrument design and intended conditions of use. ObjectiveTo evaluate the mechanical performance associated with an 8 N slip-resistance specification for the locked handle-shaft interface of an articulated laparoscopic instrument using a controlled bench model. MethodsA bench-based mechanical evaluation method was designed using the instrument under test, mechanical fixtures, a calibrated force-measurement device, and displacement-measurement equipment. After engagement of the handle-shaft locking mechanism, external forces were applied to evaluate resistance to relative displacement. Testing included axial loading, loading in relevant transverse directions, and repeated locking-unlocking cycles. The primary outcome was the force corresponding to the onset of relative slippage at the locked interface. Secondary outcomes included displacement under load, complete locking failure, and changes in mechanical performance after repeated operation. Acceptance criteria should be established before confirmatory testing. ResultsAll 30 instruments from three production batches met the 8 N axial requirement (30/30). The axial slip-onset force was 12.40 {+/-} 0.97 N (range, 10.80-14.00 N). Under a sustained load of 8 N for 60 s, mean relative displacement increased from 0.06 mm to 0.10 mm, and mean residual displacement was 0.02 mm. After 1,000 cycles, the axial slip-onset force was 12.00 {+/-} 0.97 N (range, 10.40-13.60 N). ConclusionsThis study provides a bench-testing framework for evaluating an 8 N slip-resistance specification for the handle-shaft locking interface of an articulated laparoscopic instrument. Whether this specification provides adequate mechanical stability can be determined only by comparing the measured performance with engineering acceptance criteria established in advance on the basis of the instruments intended use and foreseeable loading conditions.

papers.title: Stage-specific overall survival with complete five-year follow-up after D2 gastrectomy for gastric cancer at a referral hospital in Shanghai, China: a reference for comparing hospitals
papers.abstract: BackgroundComparing long-term outcomes of gastric cancer surgery between hospitals requires a common reference. Risk-adjusted benchmarks depend on the model and population used to build them and are difficult for another hospital to reproduce. TNM stage is a prognostic classification already recorded for every resected gastric cancer. We report unadjusted stage-specific overall survival from a consecutive cohort with complete follow-up as reference data and propose a minimal dataset for producing comparable figures elsewhere. MethodsThe cohort comprised 690 consecutive eligible patients who underwent curative-intent D2 gastrectomy for stage I to III adenocarcinoma at Ruijin Hospital, Shanghai, in 2019. All operations were performed by eight experienced, high-volume consultant surgeons. Stage followed the AJCC 8th edition: pTNM after upfront surgery (n = 570) and ypTNM after neoadjuvant chemotherapy (n = 120). Overall survival was estimated by the Kaplan-Meier method without adjustment. ResultsThere were 199 deaths, 181 within five years. Every survivor was followed for at least 68.1 months. After upfront surgery, five-year overall survival was 95.0% (95% CI 91.4 to 97.1) for stage I, 83.8% (76.5 to 89.0) for stage II and 56.5% (49.2 to 63.1) for stage III, and was 95.0% in IA and 95.2% in IB, falling to 26.7% in IIIC. After neoadjuvant chemotherapy, five-year survival was 78.6%, 61.9% and 31.3% for ypStage I, II and III. Pooling pTNM and ypTNM lowered stage III five-year survival to 50.2%. The proposed minimal dataset has 16 items, 13 of them recorded during the admission for gastrectomy. ConclusionsThese figures are intended as a reference for comparing hospitals rather than as a standard of care. We propose 16 items, most of them routinely recorded, from which another hospital can produce the same table and compare its results by stage.

papers.title: Hiporfin (HpD) for fluorescence-guided resection of recurrent glioblastoma: diagnostic accuracy and feasibility of an integrated photodynamic strategy
papers.abstract: BackgroundHematoporphyrin derivative (HpD, Hiporfin) is used for photodynamic therapy (PDT) of solid tumors but had never been evaluated for fluorescence-guided resection (FGR) in glioma. We assessed Hiporfin fluorescence accuracy against histopathology in recurrent glioblastoma (rGBM) and the feasibility of adding cavity PDT to FGR. MethodsIn this prospective single-arm study, adults with rGBM received a single preoperative intravenous Hiporfin dose of 5 mg/kg before FGR under blue-light excitation and 630-nm cavity PDT. Intraoperative fluorescence assessment was the index test and histopathology the reference standard. Specimen-level diagnostic accuracy was pooled with bivariate random-effects modeling. ResultsOf 63 specimens, 35 were true positive, 7 false positive, 8 false negative and 13 true negative. Pooled sensitivity was 0.751 (95% confidence interval 0.600-0.858) and specificity 0.606 (0.407-0.775); the crude positive predictive value was 0.833 (0.694-0.917) and the negative predictive value 0.619 (0.409-0.792). All seven false-positive specimens were peritumoral tissue and the eight false negatives were non-fluorescent tumor. FGR combined with cavity PDT was completed in all six patients without new neurological deficits. ConclusionsHiporfin fluorescence identified rGBM with moderate accuracy: fluorescent regions were likely tumor, while non-fluorescent tissue often still contained tumor. The main source of error was peritumoral tissue of the treated cavity, and not the drug or the optics. Hiporfin is a new fluorescence agent for glioma. One drug provides both fluorescence guidance during resection and immediate cavity PDT. Key PointsO_LIHiporfin fluorescence in recurrent glioblastoma: sensitivity 0.75, specificity 0.61. C_LIO_LIFluorescence predicted tumor with PPV 0.83, but its absence had NPV 0.62. C_LIO_LIFirst specimen-level accuracy estimated for Hiporfin fluorescence in recurrent glioblastoma. C_LI Importance of the StudyHiporfin (hematoporphyrin derivative) is used for photodynamic therapy of solid tumors, but its fluorescence had not been characterized in the operative field. We provide the first clinical fluorescence-guided resection data for this agent in glioma and pair it with immediate cavity photodynamic therapy in a single procedure. In this prospective six-patient series, pooled sensitivity was 0.75 and specificity 0.61, so more than a third of non-fluorescent specimens still contained tumor while every false-positive specimen was peritumoral tissue. That failure mode is intrinsic to reoperation in a treated cavity and not to the drug or the optics. The workflow was completed in every patient without new deficit; the one patient with both a newly diagnosed and a recurrent lesion suggests greater potential for Hiporfin in newly diagnosed glioblastoma, which warrants prospective evaluation.

papers.title: Beyond the Haematoma: Socioeconomic Deprivation and Outcomes in Chronic Subdural Hematoma in a Single-Centre Cohort Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundChronic subdural hematoma (CSDH) is common and increasing in incidence. Short-term post-surgical outcomes are good, but longer term, patients experience increased morbidity and early mortality than controls and the general population. Deprivation and ethnicity affect many health conditions, but to our knowledge, this is the first UK study investigating their association with CSDH outcomes. MethodsThis single-centre retrospective cohort study used Secondary Uses Service Admitted Patient Care Spells (SUS+ APCS) data. Adult subdural hematoma (SDH) patients admitted to St Georges Hospital, London treated with burr-hole surgery between April 2022 and April 2025 were included. Primary outcomes were initial length of stay (LoS) and days spent hospitalised in the subsequent year. Deprivation was measured using Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD). Linear regression models estimated initial LoS and subsequent days spent hospitalised by category, adjusted for factors including age, ethnicity and comorbidities. ResultsIn this single-centre cohort of 449 patients, IMD was not associated with initial LoS, but was significantly associated with subsequent time spent hospitalised. In a log-transformed linear regression model, the most deprived spent 4.5-times longer hospitalised during the year after CSDH than the least deprived (fold change = 4.45, 95% confidence interval (95%CI) 2.20 to 9.01). ConclusionsHigher neighbourhood-level deprivation was associated with time spent hospitalised following CSDH. This was robust to adjustment for potential mediating factors. This is the first UK study demonstrating health inequalities in CSDH outcomes, highlighting a need for future research to gain further insights, and to improve equity of outcomes after CSDH. What is already known on this topic?CSDH is a common sentinel health event, and risk factors include older age, alcohol misuse and taking anticoagulant or antiplatelet medications. Risk factors for poor outcomes include worse pre-morbid functional status and features of more severe CSDH. Neighbourhood-level socioeconomic deprivation is known to be associated with poor health outcomes in many conditions, including fractured neck of femur and stroke. What this study adds?This is the first UK study to identify that neighbourhood-level deprivation is associated with poorer outcomes after CSDH. We show that greater deprivation is associated with more days hospitalised during the 12 months after CSDH, indicating that the longer-term negative impacts experienced after CSDH may be exacerbated by neighbourhood-level socioeconomic deprivation. How this study might affect research, practice or policyFuture research should replicate these analyses in other regions, and investigate the underlying causal factors underling the inequalities in readmission for CSDH patients. Policy should focus on early intervention to mitigate risk factors for readmission, paying particular attention to those in the most deprived populations.

papers.title: Surgical Performance and Patient Outcomes in Robot-Assisted Esophagectomy: A Crowd-Sourced Video-Based Assessment
papers.abstract: BackgroundRobust evidence linking individual surgeon technical performance to patient outcomes in complex minimally invasive surgery remains scarce. Crowd-sourced video assessment offers a scalable alternative to expert review, but its clinical relevance in complex oncologic procedures such as robot-assisted minimally invasive esophagectomy (RAMIE) is unestablished. MethodsIn this exploratory study, video recordings of 60 consecutive RAMIE procedures performed by 7 surgeons (2018-2023) were segmented into five representative surgical steps and rated by 93 blinded crowd-raters per segment using a modified GEARS instrument. Tertiles were used to compare top-performing operations and steps against the remaining two terciles for overall and step-specific performance, and associations with perioperative outcomes were analyzed. ResultsTop-tercile overall performance was associated with significantly shorter operative time (abdominal, thoracic, and total) and less intraoperative blood loss (all p<0.05), without differences in postoperative outcomes. In exploratory step-specific analyses, top-tertile performance during infracarinal lymphadenectomy was associated with significantly fewer surgical complications (30.0% vs 60.0%; p=0.028), fewer severe surgical complications (25.0% vs 52.5%; p=0.043), and higher lymph node yield (22.8 vs 18.9; p=0.037), while the purse-string suture step showed the broadest operative-time benefit. These step-specific findings are hypothesis-generating and were not adjusted for multiple testing. ConclusionCrowd-sourced video assessment enables scalable, step-specific evaluation of surgical performance in RAMIE associated with intraoperative blood loss and operative time. Exploratory analyses suggest that the relationship between technical performance and clinical outcomes might be step-specific, with infracarinal lymphadenectomy emerging as risky step linked to postoperative morbidity. These findings support further investigation of individualized performance assessment for quality improvement and risk stratification.

papers.title: Diffusion MRI abnormalities localise the epileptogenic zone in paediatric drug-resistant epilepsy
papers.abstract: ObjectivesSeizure freedom follows surgery in 67% of children with drug-resistant epilepsy, but imaging biomarkers could improve patient selection, epileptogenic zone localisation, and outcome prediction. We assessed whether diffusion MRI abnormalities predicted seizure freedom when resected; aligned with stereo-EEG seizure-onset and interictal zones; distinguished patients with/without an identified onset zone; and localised the epileptogenic zone in MRI-negative cases. MethodsWe retrospectively studied children undergoing focal resection (n=110) or stereo-EEG (n=61) between 2015-2023, alongside healthy controls aged 6-18 (n=69), using identical 3T MRI diffusion protocols. Age- and sex-adjusted normative models generated mean diffusivity (MD) and fractional anisotropy (FA) voxelwise z-score maps to identify dominant abnormalities. In resection patients, abnormality-resection overlap was related to [≥]12-month Engel outcome. In stereo-EEG patients, z-scores were compared across seizure-onset, interictal, and uninvolved grey-matter contacts. In lesion-negative patients, abnormalities were compared with PET hypometabolism and stereo-EEG findings. ResultsGreater resection of MD abnormalities predicted seizure freedom, especially with overlap >0 (mean differences 17%, 23%; Pperm=0.0086, <0.001), and higher odds of Engel I (OR 1.31/10%; AUC 0.723; Youden threshold 36%). FA showed similar associations. Seizure-onset contacts had higher MD and lower FA z-scores than uninvolved grey matter (+0.65, -0.18; Pperm<0.001, =0.001), with interictal contacts intermediate. Abnormalities were more widespread and contralateral in patients without an identified onset zone. In lesion-negative patients, abnormalities co-localised with PET (20/28 fully, 6/28 partially) and stereo-EEG (17/24 fully, 3/24 partially). InterpretationDiffusion MRI abnormalities aligned with invasive electrophysiology, predicted seizure freedom when resected, and co-localized with PET/stereo-EEG, supporting an important role in presurgical evaluation.

papers.title: Assessment of Fairness and Bias of an Image-based Surgical Site Infection Detection AI Model
papers.abstract: BackgroundEvaluating fairness in artificial intelligence (AI) is essential before clinical implementation to prevent unintended harm across diverse patient populations. This study assesses performance differences of an image-based surgical site infection (SSI) detection model across age, gender, geography, race, and skin color. MethodsModel development/validation study using retrospective, multicenter data across surgical subspecialties from adults who submitted an image of their incision via the electronic health record within 30 days of their procedure between 2019-2024. Area under receiver operating curve (AUROC) was compared by age ( 0.09), however geographical differences were significant: lowest AUROC 0.83 (95% CI 0.77-0.88) vs. highest AUROC 0.87 (95% CI 0.84-0.89, p=0.01). Temporal validation using 4,242 images from 1,353 patients between 2022-2023 showed intact fairness across subgroups ({Delta}AUROC [≤]0.06) except geography ({Delta}AUROC [≤]0.16). ConclusionsThe model behaved fairly across age, gender, race, and skin color, however geographical differences persisted. These findings have practical implications underscoring the importance of evaluating bias in clinical AI before deployment.

papers.title: Revascularisation versus amputation for chronic limb-threatening ischaemia: a systematic review and meta-analysis of clinical outcomes and patient characteristics
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe relative merits of infrainguinal bypass and primary major lower limb amputation (MLLA) for chronic limb-threatening ischaemia (CLTI) remain uncertain, and the baseline profiles of patients selected for each strategy are poorly described. MethodsA systematic review and meta-analysis were undertaken in accordance with PRISMA 2020 and prospectively registered (PROSPERO: CRD42022356094). MEDLINE, Embase, CENTRAL, and CINAHL were searched from inception to March 2025. Prospective studies of adults with CLTI undergoing primary infrainguinal bypass or primary MLLA were eligible. Mortality, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and subsequent amputation outcomes were synthesised using random-effects meta-analysis of proportions. Baseline comorbidity profiles were also extracted. ResultsTwenty-seven studies involving 6,576 patients were included: 5,779 underwent infrainguinal bypass and 797 underwent MLLA. After bypass, pooled mortality was 3.7% at 30 days (95% CI 2.8%-4.9%, I{superscript 2} = 49.4%), 18.5% at 1 year (95% CI 15.6%-21.9%, I{superscript 2} = 62.3%), and 54.3% at 5 years (95% CI 50.5%-58.0%, I{superscript 2} = 0%). After MLLA, pooled mortality was 9.2% at 30 days (95% CI 4.1%-19.3%, I{superscript 2} = 73.5%), 28.5% at 1 year (95% CI 13.3%-51.0, I{superscript 2} = 70.8%), and 39.9% at 2 years (95% CI 0.3%-99.3, I{superscript 2} = 90.5%), although longer-term estimates were limited by sparse data and marked heterogeneity. Thirty-day MACE was 6.5% (95% CI 4.3%-9.7, I{superscript 2} = 63.5%) after bypass and 2.8% after MLLA (95% CI 0.1%-37.6%, I{superscript 2} = 0%). Early subsequent major amputation after bypass occurred in 3.9% of patients (95% CI 2.0%-7.7%, I{superscript 2} = 91.2%), rising to 16.2% at 1 year (95% CI 12.6%-20.5%, I{superscript 2} = 82.0%) and 33.3% at 3 years (95% CI 20.1%-49.8%, I{superscript 2} = 0%). Early re-amputation after MLLA occurred in 10.9% of patients (95% CI 4.5%-24.4%, I{superscript 2} = 40.3%). Baseline comorbidity burden was high in both groups, with substantial heterogeneity across studies. ConclusionsCLTI carries a poor prognosis regardless of treatment strategy. Infrainguinal bypass is associated with lower early mortality and better early limb preservation than primary MLLA, but long-term survival remains poor and later limb failure is common. Primary MLLA is not a low-risk alternative. Better contemporary comparative evidence utilising modern causal inference approaches is needed to support individualised decision-making.

papers.title: Large language model-augmented implicit surgical video review
papers.abstract: Surgical video interpretation is a promising medical artificial intelligence application. However, no existing video annotation method preserves the spatiotemporal complexity of surgeon reasoning. Here we show that verbal reasoning and visual attention can be converted into structured, machine-actionable records of intraoperative behaviours. Our method decomposes transcribed verbal commentary into video-anchored semantic feedback chunks, which are classified via a large language model, with spatial grounding to surgical scenes via eyegaze or cursor tracking. We demonstrate method validity and scalability on structured and unstructured annotation tasks. For quality feedback on full-length colorectal procedures, the method reached near-human fidelity for chunking (cosine similarity: 0.95{+/-}0.01) and semantic classification across observations (Cohens {kappa}: 0.71{+/-}0.07) and evaluative triggers (Cohens {kappa}: 0.67{+/-}0.14), with excellent usability ratings. For structured critical view of safety assessment in laparoscopic cholecystectomy, implicit annotation yielded excellent agreement with explicit reviewer ratings (Cohens {kappa}: 0.83, 0.49 and 0.81 across three criteria). We anticipate this method will advance surgical data science by enabling scalable construction of meaningfully annotated surgical video datasets.

papers.title: Burr-Hole Intersection of Middle Meningeal Artery Branches and Recurrence in Chronic Subdural Haematoma: a Multicentre Retrospective Cohort Study
papers.abstract: Background and ObjectivesRecurrence following burr-hole drainage of chronic subdural haematoma (cSDH) occurs in 10-25% of cases, sustained by neovascularisation of the subdural neomembrane supplied by the middle meningeal artery (MMA). MMA embolisation reduces recurrence; whether incidental burr-hole intersection of MMA branches during drainage confers similar benefit is unknown. MethodsWe performed a multicentre retrospective cohort study of consecutive adults undergoing burr-hole drainage for cSDH at two UK tertiary neurosurgical centres. Postoperative thin-slice CT was used to classify burr-hole intersection of the underlying MMA groove (no hit, distal-branch hit or main-branch hit) and measure perpendicular burr-hole-to-MMA-groove distance. Co-primary outcomes were radiological recurrence and recurrence requiring intervention. Patient-clustered multivariable logistic regression adjusted for prespecified clinical covariates and treating site. Results227 patients (284 operated hemispheres) were included. Radiological recurrence decreased from 34.4% with no branch hit to 22.9% with main-branch intersection, with the gradient confined predominantly to unilateral cSDH. Main-branch intersection was associated with lower adjusted odds of radiological recurrence in unilateral cSDH (adjusted OR 0.30, 95% CI 0.11-0.81; P = .018), with a similar but non-significant association in the overall cohort (adjusted OR 0.53, 95% CI 0.26-1.07; P = .075). Burr-hole-to-MMA-groove distance demonstrated a more consistent association: in the overall cohort, each 5-mm increase independently increased the odds of radiological recurrence (adjusted OR 1.38, 95% CI 1.04-1.82; P = .025). In unilateral cSDH, each 5-mm increase was independently associated with both radiological recurrence (adjusted OR 1.45, 95% CI 1.03-2.04; P = .034) and recurrence requiring intervention (adjusted OR 1.52, 95% CI 1.05-2.20; P = .027). ConclusionMain-branch intersection of the middle meningeal artery during routine burr-hole surgery is associated with lower recurrence of unilateral cSDH, while the accompanying burr-hole-to-MMA-groove distance gradient provides biologically plausible support for a dose-response relationship. Together, these findings provide mechanistic rationale for prospective evaluation of intentional neuronavigation-guided MMA targeting (BURR-MMA; NCT07549893).

papers.title: Beyond Length of Stay: Patient and Carer Perspectives on Virtual Hospital Pathways Following Colorectal Surgery
papers.abstract: BackgroundVirtual hospital (VH) pathways support early discharge through remote monitoring, but limited evidence has hindered implementation in colorectal surgery. This study aimed to define patient-and carer-relevant outcomes and experiences of VH following colorectal surgery. MethodologyA patient and public involvement and engagement (PPIE) consultation was conducted with 8 participants (7 patients, 1 carer; 4 women, 4 men) who had experienced VH following bowel resection at a high-volume robotic unit. Purposive sampling ensured that 50% of participants had experienced readmission. The 90-minute session was delivered via Microsoft Teams. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. ResultsSeven themes were identified: readmission, remote monitoring, carer burden, recovery, equity, readiness for discharge, and information delivery. Patients supported early discharge when remote monitoring enabled timely detection of complications and readmission pathways were efficient. Readmission was not perceived as failure but as appropriate escalation. Dissatisfaction with readmission was related to delays in emergency care. Remote monitoring provided psychological safety, with patients feeling "held" at home. Carers assumed substantial, often unrecognised, quasi-clinical roles. Recovery was defined by return to function rather than length of stay. Equity concerns were evident, with VH favouring those with adequate support at home, digital literacy, and language proficiency. Discharge readiness was both clinical and psychological. Information delivery at discharge was often poorly retained and requires reinforcement preoperatively at every encounter with patients and carers. ConclusionsVH pathways are acceptable and valued. Readmission is a marker of system responsiveness rather than failure of early discharge on VH. Psychological preparedness, carer support, and equitable access are critical to successful and scalable implementation of early discharge using a virtual hospital.

papers.title: Cohort profile: KaroLiver, a population-based cohort of patients receiving curative liver-directed treatment for colorectal liver metastases at a Swedish tertiary centre
papers.abstract: PurposeThe Karolinska Liver Metastases (KaroLiver) cohort was established to investigate associations between clinical characteristics and histopathological features in patients treated with curative intent for colorectal cancer liver metastases (CRLM). The cohort combines whole-slide digital histopathology images with detailed oncological, surgical, radiological and survival data, enabling comprehensive analyses of treatment trajectories, clinical outcomes and metastatic tumour biology. ParticipantsKaroLiver is a retrospective observational cohort comprising all consecutive patients who received curative-intent, liver-directed treatment for CRLM at Karolinska University Hospital in Stockholm, Sweden. The hospital is the primary regional referral centre for HPB surgery, serving the population of approximately 2.5 million people in the Stockholm-Gotland healthcare region. Patient enrolment is continuously updated in accordance with amended ethical approvals and evolving scientific questions. The cohort currently comprises 811 patients who underwent 1204 liver interventions between February 2012 and January 2022. Detailed clinical, oncological, surgical, pathological, molecular, recurrence and survival data are collected. Findings to dateMedian overall survival (OS) in the current cohort is 51.0 months (95% CI 46.2-57.1 months), and median recurrence-free survival (RFS) is 10.4 months (95% CI 9.2-11.9 months). The five-year OS rate is 44.9% (95% CI 41.2-48.8%). Studies using the cohort have so far identified a liver injury-derived stromal capsule in a subset of metastases, associated with improved survival. The cohort has also enabled the identification of histopathological markers of tumour biology, sex-based differences in treatment and survival, and associations between post-hepatectomy liver failure and oncological outcomes. Future plansCurrent research priorities include advanced histology-based prognostic scoring, sex differences in recurrence and retreatment, tumour biology and outcomes in early-onset versus average-onset CRLM, as well as CT- and MRI-based radiomics, all integrated within KaroLivers histopathological framework. Data sharing is supported, given that regulatory requirements are met. Retrospective accrual and outcome updates will continue for current and future studies, subject to the required approvals. Strengths and limitations of this study{square} Selection bias in KaroLiver is minimised through consecutive, population-based accrual of all patients receiving curative-intent liver-directed treatment for CRLM at a high-volume Swedish tertiary centre. {square}Granular data on recurrence, including site, timing, and intent of retreatment, enable detailed analyses of disease trajectories beyond the index hepatectomy. {square}KaroLiver is linked to CT and MRI examinations from diagnosis through recurrence; combined with detailed histopathological and molecular pathology data, this provides a platform for translational research, based on specific, defined research questions. {square}The observational design limits causal inference, and changes in treatment strategies and follow-up protocols over the study period may introduce temporal confounding that must be accounted for in analyses. {square}Molecular data, including RAS/RAF mutation status and mismatch repair status, are incomplete, reflecting real-world clinical practice and the gradual adoption of tumour profiling over the study period.

papers.title: Sampling of the Lung Microbiome in Patients Undergoing Lung Resection
papers.abstract: BackgroundAlthough the lung is of low biomass, it harbors a diverse and dynamic microbiome that may influence disease and healing. Existing studies have used diverse sampling methods with high propensities for contamination and sampling error, leading to diverse and unclear results. Here, we characterized the lung microbiome via airway and parenchymal samples to determine variation across patients and sampling methods. MethodsWe recruited adult patients undergoing lung resection for suspected or confirmed malignancy. After resection and under sterile conditions, a 1 cm cubic piece of non-cancerous lung parenchyma and a swab from the specimens bronchus were collected and sent for microbiome analysis via 16S rRNA gene amplicon (V4) sequencing on an Illumina platform. An established bioinformatics pipeline was used to determine taxonomic identification. Baseline clinical and demographic data were compared to microbiome composition. ResultsA total of 86 patients were included in the study. Beta diversity (microbial composition) varied significantly by sampling method (biopsy of lung parenchyma versus airway swabs), so all further results were analyzed within sample types. Further analyses revealed significant differences in beta diversity by lobe of the lung, indicating a different microbial composition by anatomic location. Analyses of patient demographics revealed significant differences by age and comorbidities, including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and atrial fibrillation. ConclusionsThe lung harbors a diverse microbiome that differs by anatomic location and patient characteristics. This study provides a framework for more accurate future lung microbiome sampling and characterization.

papers.title: Patient-Specific Adaptations in ERAS for High-Altitude Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy: The PAERS Hypothesis
papers.abstract: BackgroundERAS protocols reduce hospital stay by 1.88 days and complications by 29% globally, but their "one-size-fits-all" paradigm--validated at sea level--may fail at high altitude where chronic hypoxia and population-specific genetic adaptations remodel baseline physiology. No study has quantified ERAS effect weight shifts at high altitude or proposed a theoretical model to explain the gap. ObjectivesTo evaluate three dimensions of plateau ERAS remodeling--(i) risk factor weight shift, (ii) traditional marker failure, (iii) genetic background modification--and propose the PAERS (Plateau Adaptation-ERAS Remodeling Syndrome) risk stratification model tailored to altitude. MethodsRetrospective cohort of 612 adults undergoing elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy (2018-2023) at Qinghai Red Cross Hospital (2260 m). Three analytical tiers: (1) multivariable regression comparing risk factor coefficients against plain-altitude benchmarks; (2) restricted cubic spline and interaction modeling for Hb, SpO2, and LOS; (3) inferential genetic modifier analysis using population-level EPAS1 carrier rates. Primary outcomes: LOS and complication rate. ResultsThree-dimensional shift was observed: (1) Weight Remodeling: BMI replaced sex as primary risk factor (OR = 1.86, P < .001), surgeon variability amplified (F = 6.33 vs plain benchmark 2-4, an [~]58% increase in F-statistic ratio, P < .001); (2) Marker Failure: Hb showed J-type relationship with LOS (Hb x SpO2 interaction {beta} = -0.0095, P = .009), with effect reversal across SpO2 strata ("Plateau Hemoglobin Paradox"); (3) Genetic Modification (population-level inference): [~]70% EPAS1 carrier rate (range 57-85% across studies) suggests HIF-2 pathway is a baseline modifier that must be accounted for. Three falsifiable predictions were proposed. ConclusionsHigh-altitude ERAS faces three challenges: effect weight remodeling, biomarker failure, and genetic background calibration. The PAERS hypothesis proposes an integrated risk stratification model--shifting from "one-size-fits-all" to altitude-aware, patient-specific protocols.

papers.title: The Plateau Hemoglobin Paradox: Reversed Effect of Hemoglobin on Surgical Outcomes by Oxygen Saturation Strata at High Altitude
papers.abstract: BackgroundHemoglobin (Hb) elevation is the hallmark of high-altitude adaptation, yet its effect on surgical outcomes may depend on arterial oxygen saturation (SpO2)--previously uninvestigated. ObjectivesTo explore whether preoperative Hb effect on postoperative length of stay (LOS) after laparoscopic cholecystectomy (LC) reverses across SpO2 strata. MethodsRetrospective single-center cohort of 612 adults undergoing elective LC (2018-2023) at Qinghai Red Cross Hospital, Xining, China (2260 m). Exposure: preoperative Hb (82-233 g/L) and SpO2 (86%-99%), stratified as low ( =96%). Primary analysis: multivariable linear regression with Hb x SpO2 interaction, adjusted for BMI, age, sex, season. ResultsAmong 612 patients (65.8% female; mean age 43.5 [11.9] years; mean Hb 151.4 [20.7] g/L; mean SpO2 94.6% [2.3%]), the Hb x SpO2 interaction was significant (beta = -0.0095; P = .009). Hb effect reversed: in SpO2 >=93%, each 1 g/L Hb prolonged LOS by 0.003 days (P = .079); in SpO2 =180 g/L had longer LOS (1.88 vs 1.62 days; P = .001; d = 0.54). Five computational robustness analyses confirmed the interaction (leave-one-out: 100% P < .05 across 612 iterations). ConclusionsIn this exploratory cohort, we observed an SpO2-dependent reversal of the Hb effect on postoperative LOS, designated the "Plateau Hemoglobin Paradox." Given single-center design and power of 0.754, findings require replication. If replicated, this pattern may inform future perioperative risk stratification at high altitude.

papers.title: Automated Detection of Extrahepatic Bile Duct Stones on Intraoperative Cholangiography Using Deep Learning
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo evaluate the case-level performance of deep-learning segmentation models for detecting extrahepatic bile duct stones on representative intraoperative cholangiography images (IOC) and to characterize the completeness of individual-stone localization. BackgroundRetained bile duct stones can cause biliary obstruction, cholangitis, and pancreatitis. However false-positive interpretation of filling defects may prompt additional downstream procedures. Computer vision has been applied to biliary anatomy recognition and IOC adequacy assessment, but patient-level stone detection and individual-stone localization remain insufficiently studyed. MethodsRepresentative IOC images were annotated for extrahepatic biliary anatomy and stones, with case-level stone status established using a composite clinical reference standard. Two deep-learning models were developed to delineate the common bile duct and common hepatic duct and to detect and localize stones. Case-level diagnostic performance was evaluated against the composite clinical reference standard, and individual-stone localization was evaluated against expert-reviewed annotations. ResultsOn the held-out 125 patients test set, MiT-B2-UNet identified 23 of 25 stone-positive cases and 95 of 100 stone-negative cases, corresponding to a sensitivity of 0.920, specificity of 0.950, and AUC of 0.986. nnU-Net identified 19 of 25 stone-positive cases and 98 of 100 stone-negative cases, corresponding to a sensitivity of 0.760, specificity of 0.980, and AUC of 0.959. At the individual-stone level, MiT-B2-UNet and nnU-Net localized 31 of 59 and 25 of 59 annotated stones, respectively; all annotated stones were localized in 13 of 25 and 12 of 25 stone-positive cases. ConclusionsDeep-learning models can identify stone-positive IOC cases and localize individual stones. This technology may help interpreting the IOCs and reduce retained stones and unnecessary downstream interventions.

papers.title: Operative Time Heterogeneity in Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy at High Altitude: Surgeon Variability as a Modifiable Factor under Hypoxic Stress
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo quantify inter-surgeon heterogeneity in operative efficiency of laparoscopic cholecystectomy (LC) at high altitude and identify independent determinants of operative time. MethodsA single-center retrospective cohort study at the participating hospital (2,260 m altitude) included 591 elective LC cases by 7 surgeons (2020-2023). One-way ANOVA, multivariate regression with log-transformed operative time, nested model comparison, and ICC quantified surgeon versus baseline factor contributions. This study followed the STROBE (Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology) reporting guidelines [16]; the checklist is provided in the supplementary materials. ResultsInter-surgeon operative time differed significantly (F = 7.16, P < 0.001, 2 = 0.069), with 12.64 min (24.0%) gap between fastest and slowest surgeons. Regression (Adj R2 = 0.075, P < 0.001) identified age ({beta} = 0.0029/yr, P = 0.009), male sex ({beta} = 0.063, P = 0.019), and surgeon identity (Surgeon G {beta} = 0.244, P < 0.001; Surgeon F {beta} = 0.233, P = 0.001; Surgeon E {beta} = 0.214, P = 0.018) as independent predictors. BMI showed a trend (P = 0.069). Nested comparison showed surgeon factors explained 2.02-fold more variance than all baseline factors combined ({Delta}R2 = 0.063 vs R2 = 0.031; ICC = 0.074). The F-statistic exceeded the F {approx} 2-4 range reported in plain-cohort LC studies. ConclusionSurgeon variability is the dominant modifiable determinant of operative time heterogeneity in high-altitude LC, contributing 2.02-fold more variance than patient baseline factors. Standardization of surgical technique represents a potentially important intervention target for efficiency improvement.

papers.title: Modular Robotic NOSES-II for Mid-Rectal Cancer: A Preliminary Feasibility Study of a Structured Surgical Procedure
papers.abstract: Background and ObjectivesRobotic-assisted natural orifice specimen extraction surgery (NOSES) is a minimally invasive approach for mid-rectal cancer, but it is technically complex and lacks a standardized operational framework. This study aimed to propose and preliminarily validate a structured modular robotic NOSES-II surgical procedure for mid-rectal cancer. MethodsThis was a retrospective observational study that consecutively enrolled 11 patients with mid-rectal cancer who underwent modular robotic NOSES-II surgery at our center between December 2024 and August 2025. All procedures were performed by the same surgical team strictly following the predefined six-module structured surgical protocol. Perioperative indicators, pathological outcomes, and patient-reported outcomes (PROs) at 4-8 months postoperatively were collected. Key techniques were analyzed via high-definition surgical videos. ResultsAll 11 procedures were completed successfully without conversion to open surgery. The mean operative time was 299.6 {+/-} 54.2 minutes, and the mean intraoperative blood loss was 94.1 {+/-} 50.6 mL. The mean number of harvested lymph nodes was 17.4 {+/-} 8.4, with a 100% R0 resection rate. No severe complications (Clavien-Dindo grade [≥] III) occurred. The mean postoperative hospital stay was 8.2 {+/-} 1.5 days. Postoperative PROs indicated good defecatory function, urinary function, and overall quality of life. ConclusionsPreliminary findings demonstrate that the structured modular robotic NOSES-II procedure is safe and feasible for the treatment of mid-rectal cancer. This modular protocol provides a clear and reproducible technical framework for this complex procedure, and it is expected to achieve favorable functional preservation while ensuring oncological radicality.

papers.title: Improvements in Family Member Quality of Life Following a Task-Shifted Psychosocial Intervention for Road Traffic Injury Survivors in Cameroon
papers.abstract: BackgroundRoad traffic injuries (RTI) -related trauma is associated with heavy psychosocial burdens for family members involved as informal caregivers after the event. Little is known about the quality of life (QoL) experience of family members of RTI survivors in sub-Saharan Africa. This study investigated the QoL outcomes of family members after the administration of the Friendship Bench psychosocial intervention among RTI survivors in Cameroon. MethodsA pre-post study design was utilized in two trauma centers in Cameroon. The relatives underwent assessment both at baseline (Session 1) and follow-up sessions (Session 6) using the WHOQOL-BREF tool, without being exposed to any intervention. The domain scores were scaled from 0 to 100. Statistical analysis consisted in paired t-tests/Wilcoxon signed-rank tests along with effect sizes using Cohens d. ResultsThe study involved twenty-nine participants. Baseline assessment revealed overall poor quality of life across all domains, with scores in the poor range (Social = 33.33 [IQR: 25.00-47.92]; Environmental = 34.38 [IQR: 25.78-45.31]; Psychological = 45.83 [IQR: 34.38-50.00]; Physical = 46.43 [IQR: 39.29-56.25]). These scores had a statistically significant increases across all domains after the intervention (p < 0.001), accompanied by medium to large effect sizes (Cohens d:Social = 1.35; Environmental = 1.57; Psychological = 1.46; Physical = 0.73). The relationship type was found to predict social QoL (F(6,22) = 4.57, p = 0.004), with children of patients demonstrating the greatest gains. ConclusionFamily members of RTI survivors showed a significant improvement in QoL during the Friendship Bench intervention. These results highlight the importance of evaluating family member outcomes in task-shifted psychosocial programs in LMICs.
